li.a: Freotopia: Martha Rendell, entry in the Fremantle people index
Murderpedia: Martha Rendell, with reproduced accounts of the investigation and trial
Amy's Crypt: The Haunted Fremantle Prison, Western Australia

content.p: On 6 October 1909, at eight in the morning, Martha Rendell was hanged at Fremantle Prison for the wilful murder of a 14-year-old boy. The boy was Arthur Morris, the son of the man she lived with in East Perth. She had been convicted of his death twenty days before. Two other Morris children, Annie and Olive, had died in the same house in the preceding months and are described as victims she was suspected of killing. The prosecution said she had swabbed the children's throats with hydrochloric acid until they could no longer swallow. She said she had been treating them for diphtheria, and she went to the gallows saying she was innocent.

Rendell remains the last woman hanged in Western Australia. Her trial was fast, the proof was contested even then, and historians still argue about how much the verdict owed to evidence and how much to what Perth thought of a woman who lived with a man who was not her husband.
content.h2: A household that was not what it seemed
content.p: Accounts of her early life are thin. She was born on 10 August 1871 and lived in Adelaide, South Australia, where she knew Morris. She left a family there, and the sources disagree on the details: Freotopia speaks of a husband and several children, while an academic study reproduced on Murderpedia describes three children born outside marriage and a long affair with a married man, Thomas Nicholls Morris, a carpenter with a wife and nine children. Both agree that she followed him west to Perth.

When Morris and his wife separated, he was given custody of five of the youngest children, and Rendell set up home with him in a run-down cottage in East Perth. The sources do not agree on when. The academic study has the couple arrive in Perth around 1900 and move into the cottage in 1906. Freotopia says Rendell joined Morris there in 1907. Either way, the arrangement was a secret. Divorce was costly and scandalous, and living together unmarried was widely condemned. Rendell passed as Mrs Morris and the children were told to call her "Mother". Their real mother lived elsewhere and, according to the study, did not see the surviving children again until 1909.

The study describes a house of poverty and isolation: Morris away at work, Rendell alone with five children, and neighbours who might find out her secret. One account says she brutally abused the children and once beat Annie so badly that the girl could not walk. These are allegations in that account, not findings of the court.

In April 1907 a diphtheria epidemic was moving through Perth, and the four youngest Morris children, Olive, Annie, George and Arthur, all fell ill. The family doctor, James Cuthbert, later a witness against Rendell, visited regularly and, according to the academic study, praised her for nursing the children through it at the cost of her own health.

Annie then relapsed. The sources differ on her age: seven in one account on Murderpedia, nine in the academic study. All say she died in July 1907, and one gives the date as 28 July. The study says Cuthbert recorded the cause as epilepsy and cardiac weakness. The other account says the certificate named diphtheria.

In August 1907 Olive, George and Arthur were diagnosed with typhoid. Olive, aged five, died in October 1907, on 6 October according to one account. The study says her death certificate gave haemorrhage and typhoid, while another account says diphtheria. Arthur, 14, took longer to succumb. He died on 6 October 1908, exactly a year after Olive and exactly a year before Rendell would be hanged.

Cuthbert asked for an autopsy on Arthur. Two accounts agree that Rendell was present. A blog essay on Murderpedia says she called a halt part-way through, which the prosecution later argued was to stop the doctors reaching the throat, while she said they had cut enough. That essay says the partial autopsy found ulceration of the bowel, haemorrhage and cardiac failure, and that someone was suspicious enough to raise it with higher authorities but no further action followed.

George Morris, the second son, set the inquiry in motion. In one account, he went missing in early April 1909, and detectives found him at his mother's house. He told them he had run away because his stepmother had killed his brother and sisters and was trying to poison him with spirits of salts. He had complained of a sore throat after a cup of tea. An essay on Murderpedia disputes the usual telling: it says the boys were reunited with their mother in May 1909, that George went to live with her, and that his father raised the alarm.

The police inquiry, in which Harry Mann and Constable Lamond took part, was slow. The deaths were long past, and doctors could not say what swabbing with spirits of salts would do to a child. Detectives learned that Rendell had bought large quantities of spirits of salts while the children were ill and none since the last death. A neighbour told them she had seen Rendell swabbing Arthur's throat through a window and had heard his screams. On a visit, the neighbour said, she smelled the bottle and felt strong fumes and burning, and Rendell told her a doctor had prescribed it.

The bodies of the three children were exhumed on 3 July 1909. One account says diluted hydrochloric acid was found on the throat tissue. Another says autopsies showed a poison that had inflamed and caused bleeding in the bowel. Mann, lacking any scientific record of the effects, persuaded the Department of Health to test swabbing on rabbits and guinea pigs. One account says the tests showed the effects seen at autopsy. The academic study says the symptoms could not be reproduced in those experiments and that the doctors explained this by Rendell's cunning.

The trial came soon after the case of Alice Mitchell, who ran a baby farm in Perth. Reports alleged that 37 children had died in her care, and a jury found her guilty of wilful neglect causing death of one infant. She was sentenced to five years' hard labour and was still in the women's division of Fremantle Prison when Rendell arrived. The study notes that the judge in that case, Justice Macmillan, cleared a doctor who had signed numerous death certificates. It suggests this set the tone for how doctors were treated at the Rendell trial.

Press coverage cast Rendell as a "Scarlet Woman" and a "Wicked Stepmother". The study argues that the public's reaction was fuelled as much by her breach of domestic ideals as by the deaths: she had left her own children, lived in secret with a married man and, as a stepmother, fitted a figure of folk horror.

Both Rendell and Morris were charged with murder, and the trial opened in mid-September 1909 before Justice Macmillan and an all-male jury. No motive was found beyond what the investigation account calls her infatuation with Morris and her anger when the children disobeyed. Freotopia says the jury heard that she was a "sadist and pervert", and that the judge called her a "moral deformity".

The study says the defence was given a single day and called no witnesses. Morris was acquitted. One account says that although he bought spirits of salts, he was believed to have known nothing until after the deaths; he had, however, lied to police and the coroner, and the jury wanted to convict him as an accessory after the fact, which the court did not allow. The academic study argues he was spared partly because the court could not believe his own sons would give evidence against him, and partly because the court assumed Rendell was the dominant partner. Rendell was found guilty and sentenced to death. The jury made no recommendation of mercy.

The Murderpedia pages give Arthur's death as the one for which she was convicted. Freotopia says she was convicted of one death despite the lack of a motive. The deaths of Annie and Olive are described as suspected.

The study says the hanging came twenty days after the verdict and about seven weeks after the coronial inquiry sent her for trial. Thirty-eight years had passed since a woman was last executed in Western Australia, and the study counts her as the third woman hanged in the state and the only one executed for child murder.

A small group tried to save her: Labor politicians, her lawyers, reporters and her spiritual adviser, Reverend Thomas Allan. They took petitions and delegations to the Premier and the Governor, but the Executive Council refused to overturn the sentence. On the eve of the hanging, the Labor member Thomas Walker told Parliament that "execution goes with savagery not civilisation. If this woman is guilty then let her suffer life." The study says the women's organisations of Perth, convinced of her guilt, stayed silent. A blog essay notes that hardly anyone thought her innocent, though many felt hanging was too severe. She died protesting her innocence, and the investigation account says she never showed remorse.

Freotopia notes that many claimed at the time she did not get a fair trial, and that the debate occasionally resumes. The academic study calls for a retrospective pardon. A blog essay on Murderpedia goes further and argues she was a victim of prejudice, pointing to the lack of forensic proof and to doctors who had treated the children and were not themselves examined closely. The investigation account takes the opposite view and calls the case one of the most extraordinary and horrific seen by Western Australia's police. These are opinions about a case in which no court has since reviewed the verdict.

Rendell is buried in Fremantle Cemetery, in the same grave where the killer Eric Edgar Cooke was laid more than half a century later. A legend says her face can be seen in a window of the prison chapel, visible only from outside. The blog essay calls this an illusion and says a second photograph circulated as hers is almost certainly of another woman. Her story has also been told in an episode of the television series Deadly Women, titled "Pleasures For Pain".
